extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians, comedy fans, and general readers interested in comedy craft and culture
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles about writing and performing stand-up (risk-taking, bombing, targeting, authenticity, audience management) drawn from an interview with Marc Maron. Useful for performers thinking about material, boundaries, and personal storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking risks / pushing boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: “Comedy can make people uncomfortable and can push boundaries.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take risks that are calculated rather than performative. Tackling risky subjects can produce powerful, provocative comedy but may have real-world consequences — Maron notes some things in his special “could be dangerous to my life.” Choose targets and approaches thoughtfully; risk should serve the material, not just shock value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bombing and failure as part of the craft
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have really done my share of bombing. I’ve definitely done a lot of failing as a stand-up, and that’s just part of it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and accept failure as a learning tool. Repeatedly bombing is normal; use it to refine timing, material, and delivery. Embarrassment is painful but survivable — try again, iterate, and view setbacks as part of growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid punching down; don’t be an edgelord
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-woke posturing often becomes ‘a kind of cowardly ideological disposition’ and ‘a grift’ where comics punch down or trade on ignorance and bullying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid jokes that target marginalized people merely for cheap laughs. Effective boundary-pushing historically spread the discomfort across many targets (e.g., Lenny Bruce) rather than punching down. If you rely on tribal posturing to obscure lack of craft, your work will read as hackneyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality, imagination and genuine talent over tribal posturing
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re not talented, imaginative, or creative, you can ‘don the cloak of anti-wokeness’ to mask that — but that’s not real comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate comedy by its inventiveness and craft. Seek novel takes, clever construction, and original voice rather than leaning on recycled tropes or cultural grievance as a shortcut to attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance provocation with empathy
rubrics_metrics.description: You can say things people claim are off-limits ‘in a way that would provoke real humor and real empathy and a kind of balance.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing sensitive topics, aim to produce insight or empathy rather than mere transgression. Provocation should illuminate or humanize, not simply antagonize. The best risky jokes create a complex response rather than only outrage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic, specific personal storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Maron’s grief felt ‘specific’ to his experience — he didn’t consult others extensively and processed it on his own; specificity made the material powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground material in concrete, personal detail. Specificity yields resonance and avoids genericing trauma into commodity. Authentic details about a unique experience often produce stronger, more relatable comedy than broad generalized takes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and context when publicizing others’ grief
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘When someone dies, you’re not the victim. They are. … Out of respect for them, behave properly.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If making private trauma public, consider the feelings and rights of others involved (family, close relations). Avoid hogging attention or speaking in ways that disrespect those most affected; be willing to step back when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculated risks versus performative bravado
rubrics_metrics.description: Maron distinguishes taking ‘calculated risks’ from merely adopting an anti-woke posture to seem risky; the latter is often a grift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether a risky joke serves a craft purpose or is simply signaling. True risk involves meaningful stakes — e.g., interrogating powerful targets or exposing uncomfortable truths — rather than mimicking danger for branding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vulnerability for catharsis and service to others
rubrics_metrics.description: Maron chose to share his grief ‘mostly out of service to others, honestly. And out of respect for her.’ The sharing was cathartic and meant to help others experiencing similar pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vulnerability can be a powerful connective tool in comedy when offered with intention. Sharing personal pain can create catharsis for both performer and audience if done honestly and with awareness of impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept imperfection; ‘sloppy’ can be beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Truth of the matter is, my favorite guitar players are sloppy… I can play three or four chords with feeling… Sloppy is really beautiful.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfection is not required for emotional truth or audience connection. Embrace a roughness or imperfection that conveys feeling; technical polish should not eclipse authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iteration, practice, and audience rapport
rubrics_metrics.description: Maron recounts stopping songs, trying again, and relying on audiences who ‘afford’ him second tries; practice and audience patience enable growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated performance, rehearsal, and audience feedback to refine material. Cultivate rapport so audiences will tolerate experiments and missteps while you develop the act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t weaponize culture wars as a shield for laziness
rubrics_metrics.description: Many self-proclaimed anti-woke comedians recycle a few tropes and claim persecution instead of doing the hard work of being funny and imaginative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid leveraging perceived victimhood as a rhetorical crutch. Comedy should rest on craft, not on posturing about censorship or grievance to excuse weak material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider institutional and industry contexts when speaking publicly
rubrics_metrics.description: On the Andrea Riseborough/Academy controversy, Maron notes campaigning, moneyed interests, optics, and institutional insecurity shape outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When commenting on awards, controversies, or industry systems, understand the broader institutional dynamics at play. Public statements about such matters should account for politics and consequences beyond immediate artistic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider personal safety and consequences of material
rubrics_metrics.description: Maron acknowledges some things he says ‘could be dangerous to my life’ depending on who and how he’s talking about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh possible personal or physical consequences of naming or confronting certain people or groups. Assess whether the artistic value justifies potential personal risk, and plan responses if backlash occurs.
